newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore says economy recovering, to grow 5-7 pct.
newsitem.headline: Singapore says economy recovering, to grow 5-7 pct.

text.p: Singapore said on Thursday its economy was recovering from a slump in its core electronics industry and on track for five to seven percent growth this year.

Trade and Industry Minister Lee Yock Suan told reporters he had been heartened by the latest "book-to-bill" report from the North American semiconductor industry, which showed new orders in the key U.S. market outpacing deliveries.
"We still say five to seven percent for this year," Lee said.

"The book-to-bill ratio is positive. It shows the orders are more than the shipments. The leading indicators are also positive. That usually tells us that recovery is under way," Lee said at a ceremony to announce the construction of a new US$1 billion electronics plant.
The plant will be built by a government-backed joint venture of state-owned Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing and Hewlett-Packard of the United States.
The Singapore economy grew by seven percent in 1996, significantly below the 8.8 percent expansion of 1995 and the double-digit growth of the previous two years.
Much of the slowdown was due to a slowdown in global electronics trade, the industry which dominates the island's economy.
Electronics and computer components and related products account for almost 50 percent of Signapore's manufacturing output and around 60 percent of its non-oil exports.

Recent official figures have suggested the economic slowdown may not be over. Singapore's industrial production fell 7.2 percent in January year-on-year with electronics exports contracting 3.1 percent.
But Lee said he was confident of a recovery in the core electronics sector.
"We are confident, despite the setback," he said.
He declined to comment on the performance of the Singapore economy in the first quarter of 1997.
Lee said earlier in a speech that the Singapore government wanted to build up its electronics wafer fabrication industry.
It was a strategic industry which would provide high returns for the country's skilled but limited workforce, he said.
Wafer fabrication plants are central to the production of the micro-chips that control modern electronics.
The plants take thin round wafers of silicon, coat them with metals and print or etch on circuits. The wafers are later cut up into tiny chips for use in computers and other devices.
"Just over four years ago, Singapore had only four wafer fab plants. Today we have 10 plants that are either already in operation or under development," Lee said.
He rejected suggestions that Singapore was over-dependent on electronics and had all its industrial "eggs in one basket".
"On the whole we are still very confident of the industry and we think it is the right industry to have, especially wafer fab plants. We would like to build up our capacity in this area.
"It is really a key component of a lot of new products and advances in technology are very rapid. What we intend to have is a lot of state-of-the-art plants," he said.
"The electronics industry is really the growth sector with the advent of the micro-chip," he said.

"We do have also other sectors like the chemical industry and petrochemicals and we are pushing the other sectors as well. The fact that it is one of the biggest sectors is just a natural positive development. It is the same in any country."
